questions.stem: What does 「天気よほうによると、明日は雪がふるそうです。」 mean?
options: It looks as if it is about to snow
The forecast says it snowed yesterday
The forecast says it will not snow tomorrow
The forecast says it will snow tomorrow
questions.explanation: A plain form plus 「そうです」 reports something heard or read, and 「によると」 names the source. 'It looks as if it is about to snow' would be the verb stem plus 「そう」: 「雪がふりそうです」.

questions.stem: What is the difference between 「このケーキはおいしそうです。」 and 「このケーキはおいしいそうです。」?
options: The first is judged from its look; the second reports what someone said
The first describes the cake now; the second describes how it tasted before
The first is polite speech; the second is plain speech used with friends
The first states a certain fact; the second is only the speaker's guess
questions.explanation: An adjective stem plus 「そう」 (「おいし」 + 「そう」) is an impression from appearance: 'it looks delicious'. The full plain form plus 「そう」 (「おいしい」 + 「そう」) is hearsay: 'I hear it is delicious'. Both sentences are polite and both are in the present.

questions.stem: Which form of 「いい」 completes 「この店のラーメンは ___ そうですね。」 ('looks good')?
options: よく
いさ
よさ
いい
questions.explanation: 「いい」 is irregular before appearance 「そう」: it becomes 「よさそう」, just as 「ない」 becomes 「なさそう」. 「いいそうです」 is grammatical, but it is hearsay ('I hear it is good'), not appearance.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「田中さんは病気 ___ そうです。」 ('I hear Tanaka is ill')?
options: な
の
で
だ
questions.explanation: Hearsay 「そう」 follows a complete plain form, and the plain form of a noun sentence is 「病気だ」. 「な」 only links a な-adjective to a noun, and 「の」 links two nouns, so neither can end a clause before hearsay 「そう」.

questions.stem: What does 「来年、日本の大学に入るつもりです。」 mean?
options: I intend to enter a Japanese university next year
I am expected to enter a Japanese university next year
I hear I will enter a Japanese university next year
I might enter a Japanese university next year
questions.explanation: A plain form plus 「つもりです」 states the speaker's own intention or plan. Being expected to do something would be 「はずです」, and 'might' would be 「かもしれません」.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「お金がないので、今年は車を ___ つもりです。」 ('I plan not to buy a car this year')?
options: 買って
買わなくて
買わない
買う
questions.explanation: 「つもり」 follows a plain form, and a plan not to do something takes the plain negative: 「買わないつもりです」. 「買うつもりです」 says the opposite, and a て-form cannot come before 「つもり」.

questions.stem: You bought a camera in Melbourne just before leaving for Japan. Which form completes 「日本へ ___ とき、カメラを買いました。」?
options: 行く
行った
行って
行き
questions.explanation: Before 「とき」, the verb's tense shows whether that action had happened yet, not when the whole sentence is set. 「行くとき」 means you had not yet gone, so you bought it before leaving; 「行ったとき」 would mean you bought it in Japan after arriving.

questions.stem: What does 「私がしゅくだいをしている間に、母は晩ご飯を作りました。」 mean?
options: While I was doing my homework, my mother made dinner
Before I did my homework, my mother made dinner
After I did my homework, my mother made dinner
My mother made dinner so that I could do my homework
questions.explanation: 「間に」 places an event at some point within a period: dinner was made during the time I was doing homework. 'Before' would be 「する前に」 and 'after' would be 「した後で」.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「電車に乗っている ___、ずっと本を読んでいました。」?
options: 後で
間
間に
前に
questions.explanation: 「ずっと」 says the reading went on for the whole period, which needs 「間」 without 「に」. 「間に」 marks a single event at some point within the period, so it clashes with 「ずっと」, and 「前に」 and 「後で」 cannot follow a 「ている」 form.

questions.stem: Which words complete 「バスより電車 ___ 早いです。」?
options: のほうで
のほうに
のほうが
のほうを
questions.explanation: In a comparison the item that is more so is the subject of the adjective, so it takes 「が」: 「電車のほうが早いです」. 「を」 marks an object, and an adjective such as 「早い」 cannot take one.

questions.stem: Asked 「りんごとバナナと、どちらのほうが好きですか。」, which answer is correct?
options: 「バナナが一番好きです。」
「バナナより好きです。」
「バナナのほうを好きです。」
「バナナのほうが好きです。」
questions.explanation: A 「どちら」 question compares two things, so the answer uses 「のほうが」. 「一番」 is for the top of three or more, and 「バナナより好きです」 would mean you like something else more than bananas.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'He might be ill'?
options: 「病気のかもしれません。」
「病気かもしれません。」
「病気だかもしれません。」
「病気なかもしれません。」
questions.explanation: With nouns and な-adjectives, 「かもしれない」 attaches directly with no 「だ」: 「病気かもしれません」, 「しずかかもしれません」. Verbs and い-adjectives use their plain form: 「ふるかもしれません」, 「高いかもしれません」.

questions.stem: When does a writer use 「だろう」 instead of 「でしょう」?
options: When the writer is addressing someone of higher status
In plain-style writing such as an essay, or in casual speech
When the writer is more certain that the guess is right
When the guess is about something that happened in the past
questions.explanation: 「だろう」 is the plain form of 「でしょう」 and carries the same degree of probability. It belongs in 「だ」/「である」 writing and casual speech, while 「でしょう」 suits polite speech and 「です」/「ます」 writing.

questions.stem: What does 「夏休みに京都へ行こうと思っています。」 mean?
options: I think I went to Kyoto in the summer holidays
I think you should go to Kyoto in the summer holidays
I heard he is going to Kyoto in the summer holidays
I am thinking of going to Kyoto in the summer holidays
questions.explanation: The volitional form plus 「と思っています」 states an intention the speaker has been considering: 'I'm thinking of going'. Advice to someone else would be 「行ったほうがいい」.

questions.stem: What does 「田中さんは三時に来ると言いました。」 mean?
options: I told Tanaka that I would come at three
Tanaka said that she would come at three
Tanaka said that she had come at three
Tanaka told me to come at three
questions.explanation: Reported speech in Japanese keeps the tense of the original words, so 「来る」 is what Tanaka said ('I will come'); English shifts it to 'would come'. 'Had come' would need 「来た」, and an instruction to come would be 「来るように言いました」.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「あの先生はとてもしんせつ ___ と思います。」?
options: です
の
だ
な
questions.explanation: 「と思う」 follows a plain form, and a な-adjective in its plain form ends in 「だ」: 「しんせつだと思います」. The polite 「です」 does not go before 「と思う」, and 「な」 appears only before a noun.

questions.stem: What does 「車を買うためにお金をためています。」 mean?
options: I am saving money since cars are expensive
I am saving money in order to buy a car
I am saving money because I bought a car
I am saving money instead of buying a car
questions.explanation: A plain form plus 「ために」 gives the purpose of a deliberate action. 'Because I bought a car' would be 「買ったので」 or 「買ったから」.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「日本語が上手に話せる ___、毎日れんしゅうしています。」?
options: ようで
つもりで
ように
ために
questions.explanation: 「話せる」 is a potential form: it describes an ability, not a deliberate act, so the goal takes 「ように」. 「ために」 needs a verb the subject controls, as in 「日本語を話すために」.

questions.stem: Why does 「かぜをひかないように手を洗いましょう。」 use 「ように」 rather than 「ために」?
options: 「ために」 is used only in formal writing and never in speech
「ように」 makes the sentence an invitation, just like 「ましょう」
「ために」 would put the whole sentence into the past tense
Not catching a cold is a result you cannot directly control
questions.explanation: 「ように」 states a goal or desired state that the subject cannot simply choose, such as not catching a cold. 「ために」 gives the purpose of a deliberate action. Both are common in speech and writing, so register is not the reason.

questions.stem: What does 「先生は学生にしゅくだいを早く出すように言いました。」 mean?
options: The teacher told the students to hand in their homework early
The teacher said the students had handed in their homework early
The students told the teacher they would hand in homework early
The teacher told the students not to hand in homework early
questions.explanation: A plain form plus 「ように言う」 reports a request or instruction. A statement of fact would use 「と言いました」, and 'not to' would need the negative: 「出さないように」.

questions.stem: In 「この町は店も多いし、駅も近いし、住みやすいです。」, what does 「し」 do?
options: It lists reasons and implies there are others
It shows a contrast between the two clauses
It shows the actions happen one after another
It sets out a condition for the final clause
questions.explanation: A plain form plus 「し」 piles up reasons, often with 「も」: there are lots of shops, the station is close, and so on, so the town is easy to live in. A sequence would use the て-form, and a contrast 「が」 or 「けれども」.

questions.stem: What does 「きのう見たえいがはとてもおもしろかったです。」 mean?
options: Yesterday I saw a film with a very interesting person
The film I saw yesterday was very interesting
I saw the film yesterday because it was interesting
The film I am going to see will be interesting
questions.explanation: 「きのう見た」 is a relative clause in front of 「えいが」: 'the film (that) I saw yesterday'. Japanese puts the describing clause before the noun, with no word for 'that' or 'which'.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「春子さん ___ 作ったケーキはおいしかったです。」?
options: を
で
が
は
questions.explanation: The subject of a relative clause takes 「が」 (or 「の」), never 「は」, because 「は」 marks the topic of the whole sentence. Here the topic is the cake, and 「春子さん」 is only the subject of 「作った」.

questions.stem: Which phrase means 'the person who is wearing a red shirt'?
options: 「赤いシャツを着ているの人」
「赤いシャツが着ている人」
「赤いシャツを着ている人」
「人は赤いシャツを着ている」
questions.explanation: The relative clause 「赤いシャツを着ている」 goes straight before 「人」, with no 「の」 between a verb and the noun. 「人は…着ている」 is a full sentence ('the person is wearing'), not a noun phrase.

questions.stem: What does 「んです」 add to 「明日テストがあるんです。」?
options: It shows the speaker heard about the test from someone
It shows that the test has already finished
It presents the test as the explanation for the situation
It turns the statement into a question to the listener
questions.explanation: 「の」/「んです」 gives an explanation or background, for example why you cannot go out tonight. Hearsay would be 「あるそうです」, and a question would end in 「か」 or 「の」.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「あの人はこの学校の先生 ___ んです。」?
options: の
で
な
だ
questions.explanation: Before 「の」/「んです」, a noun or な-adjective takes 「な」 in place of 「だ」: 「先生なんです」, 「しずかなんです」. Keeping the 「だ」, as in 「先生だんです」, is a common slip.

questions.stem: What does 「だれかがここでキャンプをしたらしいです。」 mean?
options: Someone ought to camp here
Someone is about to camp here
Someone wants to camp here
Apparently someone camped here
questions.explanation: A plain form plus 「らしい」 means 'apparently' or 'it seems', a conclusion drawn from evidence or from what others say. 'Ought to' would be 「べき」, and 'about to' would be the verb stem plus 「そう」.

questions.stem: How do 「らしい」 and 「ようだ」 usually differ?
options: 「ようだ」 is used only in writing; 「らしい」 is used only in speech
「らしい」 often rests on what was heard; 「ようだ」 on what the speaker observes
「らしい」 is used only for the past; 「ようだ」 is used only for the present
「らしい」 is a firm statement of fact; 「ようだ」 is always only a guess
questions.explanation: Both mean 'it seems', but 「らしい」 leans on outside information such as reports or what others say, while 「ようだ」 gives the speaker's own judgement from what they see or experience. Both work in any tense, in speech and in writing.

questions.stem: Which ending completes 「あそこにいる人は田中さんの弟 ___。」 ('Apparently that person is Tanaka's younger brother')?
options: のらしいです
ならしいです
らしいです
だらしいです
questions.explanation: 「らしい」 attaches straight to a noun: 「弟らしいです」. Unlike 「ようだ」, which needs 「の」 after a noun (「弟のようです」), it takes neither 「の」 nor 「な」, and 「だ」 is dropped.

questions.stem: What does 「電車は8時に着くはずです。」 mean?
options: The train arrives at eight every day
The train might arrive at eight
The train is expected to arrive at eight
The train arrived at eight, I hear
questions.explanation: 「はず」 expresses what the speaker expects on reasonable grounds, such as a timetable: 'should arrive', 'is expected to'. 'Might' is 「かもしれない」, which is much less sure, and a plain statement of routine would be 「毎日8時に着きます」.

questions.stem: In a persuasive essay you want to argue that schools ought to teach more Japanese. Which sentence says this?
options: 「学校はもっと日本語を教えるべきだ。」
「学校はもっと日本語を教えるはずだ。」
「学校はもっと日本語を教えたはずだ。」
「学校はもっと日本語を教えるそうだ。」
questions.explanation: 「べき」 states what someone ought to do, the language of a persuasive argument. 「はず」 says what the speaker expects will happen, not what should happen, even though English 'should' can cover both.

questions.stem: What does 「先生が駅までの道を教えてくださいました。」 mean?
options: I asked the teacher the way to the station
The teacher kindly told me the way to the station
I told the teacher the way to the station
The teacher had me show the way to the station
questions.explanation: て-form plus 「くださる」 shows a superior doing something for the speaker's side, and it carries gratitude. The teacher is the subject, marked by 「が」, so the teacher did the telling.

questions.stem: Which sentence means 'My friend drove me to the station'?
options: 「友だちが駅まで車でおくってくれました。」
「友だちに駅まで車でおくってくれました。」
「友だちが駅まで車でおくってもらいました。」
「友だちに駅まで車でおくってあげました。」
questions.explanation: With 「てくれる」 the person doing the favour is the subject, marked by 「が」. With 「てもらう」 the receiver is the subject and the giver takes 「に」 (「友だちにおくってもらいました」), so 「友だちに…くれました」 mixes the two patterns.

questions.stem: Why is 「先生、かばんを持ってあげましょうか。」 a poor way to offer help to a teacher?
options: 「ましょうか」 cannot follow a て-form verb when making an offer
「てあげる」 stresses the favour, which sounds condescending to a superior
「てあげる」 can only be used for giving objects, never for actions
「持つ」 cannot be used in the て-form before another verb
questions.explanation: 「てあげる」 highlights that the speaker is doing the listener a favour, which is fine with friends but presumptuous towards a teacher; a humble offer such as 「お持ちしましょうか」 is used instead. 「てあげる」 with actions is normal among equals: 「買ってあげましょうか」.

questions.stem: What does 「先生に作文を見ていただきました。」 mean?
options: The teacher had me look over an essay
The teacher asked me to show her my essay
I had the teacher look over my essay
I looked over the teacher's essay for her
questions.explanation: 「ていただく」 is the humble form of 「てもらう」: the speaker receives a favour from a superior, who is marked by 「に」. The teacher did the looking, and the speaker is grateful to have had it done.

questions.stem: Which verb completes 「弟がさらを洗って ___。」 ('My younger brother did the dishes for me')?
options: あげました
もらいました
くれました
くださいました
questions.explanation: A favour done for the speaker, with the giver as subject, takes 「てくれる」. 「くださる」 is the respectful version used for superiors, which is wrong for a younger brother, and 「あげる」 would mean he did it for someone else.

questions.stem: What is the potential form of 「読む」?
options: 読まれる
読みられる
読むれる
読める
questions.explanation: う-verbs form the potential by moving the final sound to the え-row and adding 「る」: 「読む」 → 「読める」. 「読まれる」 is the passive ('be read'), and 「られる」 is added only to る-verbs.

questions.stem: What does 「漢字が百ぐらい書けます。」 mean?
options: I can write about a hundred kanji
I have written about a hundred kanji
I want to write about a hundred kanji
I have to write about a hundred kanji
questions.explanation: 「書ける」 is the potential of 「書く」, and the thing you can do is marked by 「が」. 'Have to write' would be 「書かなければなりません」, and 'want to' 「書きたいです」.

questions.stem: What is the 「ば」 conditional of 「安い」?
options: 安ければ
安いば
安くば
安かれば
questions.explanation: い-adjectives drop the final 「い」 and add 「ければ」: 「安い」 → 「安ければ」, 'if it is cheap'. 「安かったら」 is the 「たら」 equivalent, and 「安かれば」 mixes the two.

questions.stem: What does 「時間があれば、日本へ行きたいです。」 mean?
options: Even if I have time, I won't go to Japan
If I have time, I would like to go to Japan
When I had time, I went to Japan
Because I have time, I want to go to Japan
questions.explanation: 「あれば」 is the 「ば」 conditional of 「ある」: 'if there is time'. 'Even if' would be the て-form plus 「も」, 「あっても」, and 'because' would be 「から」 or 「ので」.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「日本に ___、電話してください。」 ('When you get to Japan, please call me')?
options: 着いたり
着いたら
着けば
着くと
questions.explanation: When the main clause is a request, the conditional must be 「たら」. 「と」 describes natural or habitual results and cannot be followed by a request, and 「ば」 after an action verb such as 「着く」 cannot be either.

questions.stem: Which ending correctly completes 「春になると、」?
options: 「花がさきます。」
「花見に行きましょう。」
「花見に行ってください。」
「花見に行きませんか。」
questions.explanation: 「と」 links a condition to a natural or habitual result: when spring comes, flowers bloom. It cannot be followed by a suggestion, request or invitation; for those, use 「たら」: 「春になったら、花見に行きましょう」.

questions.stem: What does 「『さくら』という店を知っていますか。」 mean?
options: Do you know a shop called Sakura?
Did someone say the shop is Sakura?
Do you know that the shop sells cherry blossoms?
Do you know where Sakura's shop is?
questions.explanation: NAME 「という」 NOUN introduces something by its name: 'a shop called Sakura'. It is used when the listener may not know the name. Sakura's shop would be 「さくらさんの店」.
